units.name: command-core
units.role: Represent a CLI program as a tree of commands and run it.
units.description: This is the heart of the library. It defines what a 'command' is (like `git` or `git commit`): its name, description, which function runs when it's invoked, and which flags it accepts. It provides the engine that reads what the user typed, walks down the tree to find the right command, checks the flags and arguments are valid, runs the command's setup/run/cleanup steps in order, and prints help or usage text when something goes wrong or is asked for. Almost everything else in this library works by calling into this engine or being called by it at the right moment. It never decides how to render a shell script or a doc page itself — it hands that work to other pieces.

units.name: args-validation
units.role: Decide whether the positional words after a command are acceptable.
units.description: This unit decides whether the extra words a user types after a command (its positional arguments, as opposed to flags like --verbose) are acceptable. It provides a small toolbox of ready-made rules — 'no arguments allowed', 'exactly two arguments required', 'between two and five arguments', 'no repeated arguments', 'only these specific words are allowed' — plus a way to combine several rules together. A command author picks one of these rules, or writes a custom one, and attaches it to a command; when the command runs, the rule is consulted to reject bad input with a helpful error message before the command's real work begins.

units.name: flag-groups
units.role: Enforce relationships between a command's flags.
units.description: This unit lets a command author declare rules about how a command's flags relate to each other: a set of flags that must all be used together, a set where at least one is required, or a set where only one may be used at a time. It provides the functions a programmer calls when defining a command to mark flags into these groups, the check that runs when the command executes to reject invalid combinations with a clear error message, and logic that adjusts shell tab-completion suggestions so they respect these same grouping rules, such as hiding flags that would conflict with one already typed.

units.name: active-help
units.role: Let a completion callback show short hint lines to the user while they type.
units.description: This is Cobra's 'Active Help' feature: a small mechanism that lets a program's own shell-completion code show short hint messages to the user while they are typing a command, for example telling them what kind of value is expected next. It provides one function programs call to attach a hint message to a list of suggested completions, a way to check whether the user or the program has turned Active Help off via an environment variable, and the shared marker text and per-program environment-variable name that every shell's completion script (bash, zsh, fish, PowerShell) uses to recognise and, if needed, silence these hints.

units.name: completion-engine
units.role: Decide what to suggest when the user presses Tab.
units.description: This unit is the decision-making brain behind Cobra's shell tab-completion feature. When a user presses Tab while typing a command, this code figures out what to suggest: which sub-commands, flags, or flag values make sense next. It provides the hidden '__complete' command that every shell's generated script calls behind the scenes, a set of flags ('directives') that tell the shell how to behave — such as 'don't add a space' or 'only show directories' — and the public functions application authors use to register custom completion logic for a command or flag, or to mark a flag as expecting a filename, a directory, or a required value. It does not know how to speak bash, zsh, fish, or PowerShell syntax itself; it hands that off to separate script-rendering units, but it decides the content those renderers will show.

units.name: bash-completion-gen
units.role: Render a command tree as a bash tab-completion script.
units.description: This code turns a program's command structure into the text of a bash shell script that gives users Tab-key autocomplete. There are two generations: an older one that writes all the completion logic directly in bash, and a newer one that writes a much smaller bash script which, at Tab-press time, calls back into the program itself via a hidden '__complete' command to ask what the valid completions are. Either way, the output is just text handed to whatever destination the caller provides — typically the console or a file on disk. It also owns the vocabulary of annotation keys (which flags want filename completion, which directory, which are required, which use a custom bash function) that the rest of the completion system reads and writes.

units.name: zsh-completion-gen
units.role: Render a command tree as a zsh tab-completion script.
units.description: This code writes out a script that lets people use the Tab key to auto-complete commands and options when using this program in the zsh shell. It walks the program's list of commands and turns them into a self-contained zsh script; that script, once installed, asks the program itself (via the hidden '__complete' command) what the valid options are each time the user presses Tab. It does not decide what the program's actual commands or flags are — it only knows how to translate that information into zsh's scripting language, plus a couple of file-writing helpers for saving the generated script to disk.

units.name: fish-completion-gen
units.role: Render a command tree as a fish tab-completion script.
units.description: This code writes a ready-to-use fish-shell script that teaches the fish shell how to offer tab-completion suggestions for a program built with Cobra. Instead of hard-coding a list of possible completions, the generated script calls back into the program itself, using the hidden '__complete' command, every time the user presses Tab, so suggestions always match the program's current commands and flags. The unit can either write this script text to any output stream or save it directly to a file on disk.

units.name: powershell-completion-gen
units.role: Render a command tree as a PowerShell tab-completion script.
units.description: This code writes out a ready-to-use PowerShell script that gives users tab-completion for a program built with Cobra. When a user runs the program's 'completion powershell' command, this generates a block of PowerShell code that, at the moment someone presses Tab, quietly re-runs the program with a hidden '__complete' instruction to ask what valid options come next, then formats and displays those suggestions. It does not decide what the valid options are — it only produces the PowerShell wrapper script that calls back into the program to find out.

units.name: template-runtime
units.role: Provide the shared toolbox — templates, feature flags, lifecycle hooks, string helpers — the rest of the library builds on.
units.description: This is the small shared toolbox that the rest of the Cobra library is built on top of. It holds global on/off switches that change how commands behave, such as whether to auto-complete abbreviated command names, whether sub-commands get sorted alphabetically, or whether to show a Windows-only warning when the program is double-clicked instead of run from a terminal. It also provides the machinery for registering custom text-template functions used when rendering help and usage screens, hooks that let a program run setup and cleanup code every time a command executes, a couple of small string-comparison helpers used for padding text and suggesting 'did you mean ...' corrections, and a 'give up and quit' helper that prints an error and exits the program. None of this code decides what a specific command does; it just supplies common conveniences the command tree and help system rely on.

units.name: doc-generators
units.role: Turn a command tree into man pages, Markdown, reStructuredText, or YAML documentation.
units.description: This code takes the tree of commands and sub-commands that make up a command-line program built with Cobra and automatically writes out human-friendly documentation for it, in four different formats: Unix man pages, Markdown, reStructuredText, and YAML. Instead of a developer manually writing and maintaining separate help documents, these functions walk through every command, read its name, description, examples, and flags, and produce ready-to-read files, or write to any output stream, so users and websites can show CLI help without reading the source code.

violations_observed.note: Reads and writes completion-engine's unexported package-level globals flagCompletionFunctions and flagCompletionMutex directly, instead of going through the exported RegisterFlagCompletionFunc/GetFlagCompletionFunc entrypoints. This is legal Go (same package) but is a direct reach into another unit's internal state rather than its declared contract. Recorded, not fixed.
